Patient-reported symptoms:

  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
# Carmen

Carmen was thirty-eight when she first sat down in a therapist's office, choosing the chair in the corner farthest from the door—a choice so automatic she did not register making it. She had come because her partner, David, had finally said the words she had been dreading: "I can't keep living like this." He meant the way she woke at two or three in the morning, rigid beside him, her body coiled as though ready to spring. He meant the way she interrogated him about his schedule, the way she kept their apartment arranged so she could see into every room from where she sat, the way she sometimes looked at him with eyes that seemed to be looking through him, searching for a threat he could not name.

The story Carmen told began in 1985, when she was seven years old. Her father came home that evening in a mood she had learned to recognize—the way he moved through the kitchen with an edge, the way his voice scraped when he spoke to her mother. Carmen had been in the living room coloring at a small table when he called her into the bedroom. She remembered the door closing behind her. She remembered his hands, the weight of him, the specific texture of the blanket beneath her—rough, wool, blue with white stripes. She remembered the ceiling, the water stain in the corner shaped like a map. After that, the memory fractured into islands: his voice, angry; her small body; the sensation of being unable to move, unable to call out. Other parts were gone entirely, dissolved into a fog she could not penetrate no matter how hard she tried. When she attempted to recall what happened after—how long it lasted, what he said, how it ended—there was only blankness, as though her mind had simply stopped recording.

For years, Carmen had carried this event in a sealed compartment. She became a high-achieving student, then a passionate community organizer working in East Los Angeles, mobilizing residents around housing rights and police accountability. Her colleagues knew her as tireless, brilliant, unflappable. What they did not know was that she was running. The work was real, the commitment was real, but it was also a machine she fed herself into—a way to keep the machinery of her mind occupied so that nothing else could surface. Nights were harder. She had come to believe that sleep was a luxury she could not afford, that the moment she closed her eyes, something catastrophic would happen. She lay awake cataloging the exits from her bedroom, listening to the ambient sounds of the apartment, waiting for the particular creak of the floorboards that would signal danger.

The triggers were diffuse but devastating. Any situation where Carmen felt cornered—a crowded bus, a meeting room with only one exit, even a conversation where she felt pressured to decide something quickly—would send her into a state of near-panic. The sensation was not fear exactly, but something closer to drowning: the absolute certainty that she had no options, that she was trapped. At those moments, the memory would arrive unbidden and vivid—not the whole event, but fragments: the blue blanket, the ceiling stain, the feeling of powerlessness that seemed to radiate from her own body like a frequency only she could hear.

What frightened her most was the numbness. There were stretches of days when she could recount what had happened to her with the flatness of someone describing a news story. The memories were there, crisp and visual, but they belonged to someone else. She felt dead inside, as though the part of her that could feel had been sealed away in that bedroom and never retrieved. She had come to believe that this numbness was the truth about her—that she was fundamentally weak, that a stronger person would have found a way to stop it, would have screamed or fought or run. The fact that she had done none of these things seemed to her like evidence of a defect so deep that no amount of professional success could repair it.

When David said he could not keep living this way, something in Carmen shifted. She realized she had been trying to erase the memory for thirty years and it had only grown sharper. She called a therapist the next morning, her hands shaking as she dialed, terrified of what might happen if she stopped running.
